procedural_history.impugned_order: Implied conviction/sentence by a lower court in Haryana
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Unknown (but implied that the High Court of Punjab and Haryana upheld the lower court's decision)
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Pradeep appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging the decision of the lower court (upheld by the High Court). The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, overturning the previous decisions.

directions: The impugned judgments of the High Court dated 12th January 2009 and the impugned judgment of the Trial Court dated 31st January 2005 are hereby set aside.
The appellant is acquitted of the offences alleged against him.
As the appellant is on bail, his bail bonds stand cancelled.

issue.issue_text: The duty of a court to conduct a proper preliminary examination of a child witness to ascertain their capacity to understand questions and give rational answers before recording their evidence.

facts: The case involved the testimony of a minor witness (PW-1), the son of the deceased.
The trial judge conducted a preliminary examination of the minor before recording his evidence.
This examination was described as "very sketchy," consisting of only three questions.
Based on this brief examination, the trial judge concluded that the witness was capable of giving answers and administered an oath.
law: It is the duty of a judicial officer to conduct a proper preliminary examination of a minor witness before recording their evidence.
The purpose of this examination is to ascertain whether the minor is capable of understanding the questions put to them and giving rational answers.
The judge must be satisfied that the child understands the questions, can respond to them, and understands the importance of speaking the truth.
It is advisable to record the preliminary questions and answers so that an appellate court can review the trial court's opinion on the witness's competency.
application: The Supreme Court found that the trial judge in this case failed to perform their duty properly.
The preliminary examination, consisting of only three questions, was deemed "very sketchy" and insufficient to properly assess the child's capacity and understanding.

The Court noted that the trial judge was required under Section 118 of the Evidence Act to record an opinion that the child could understand questions and give rational answers, which was not adequately done.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted and affirmed that it is a crucial duty of a trial court to conduct a proper and thorough preliminary examination of a child witness. This is necessary to ascertain the child's capacity to understand questions and provide rational answers before their evidence is recorded. The Court held that the trial judge in this specific case failed in this duty by conducting an insufficient examination.

issue.issue_text: Whether corroboration of the testimony of a child witness is a mandatory rule of law.

facts: The case involved a conviction that was based on the sole testimony of a minor witness (PW-1), the deceased's son.
law: The Supreme Court held that corroboration of the testimony of a child witness is not a mandatory rule of law.
Instead, it is a measure of caution and prudence.
Under Section 118 of the Evidence Act, a child is a competent witness unless the court finds they cannot understand questions or give rational answers due to their tender age.
application: The Court reasoned that while a child witness is easily susceptible to being tutored, this fact alone is not a ground to automatically reject their evidence.
Rather than imposing a rigid rule requiring corroboration, the Court emphasized the duty of the trial judge to exercise extreme care and caution.
This duty involves a careful scrutiny of the child's testimony to determine if they might have been tutored.
The judge must conduct a proper preliminary examination to ascertain if the child can understand the questions, provide rational answers, and comprehend the importance of speaking the truth.
This careful judicial scrutiny serves as the necessary safeguard, making a mandatory corroboration rule unnecessary.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that corroboration of a child witness's testimony is a mandatory rule of law, clarifying that it is a rule of caution and prudence that requires the court to carefully scrutinize the evidence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the preliminary examination of the child witness conducted by the Trial Court in the present case was adequate.

facts: The Trial Court (Sessions Judge) conducted a preliminary examination of the minor witness before taking his testimony.
This examination was described as "very sketchy" and consisted of only three questions.
Based on these three questions, the Trial Judge concluded that the witness was capable of giving answers and administered an oath to him.
law: A judge has a crucial duty to conduct a "proper preliminary examination" of a minor witness.
The purpose of this examination is to ascertain whether the minor can understand the questions asked, is capable of giving rational answers, and understands the importance of speaking the truth.
This duty is a requirement under Section 118 of the Evidence Act.
It is advisable for the trial court to record the preliminary questions and answers so that an appellate court can review the correctness of the judge's opinion.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Sessions Judge "did not do his duty" in this case.
The Court determined that an examination consisting of only three questions was "very sketchy" and insufficient to properly assess the child's competency.
This brief examination was not a "proper" or adequate way to determine if the child could understand questions, give rational answers, and appreciate the duty to tell the truth as required by law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the preliminary examination as inadequate because it was too brief and superficial. The Trial Judge failed to fulfill the legal duty to conduct a proper and thorough examination to ensure the child witness was competent to testify.

arguments.issue_text: The duty of a court to conduct a proper preliminary examination of a child witness to ascertain their capacity to understand questions and give rational answers before recording their evidence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, as supported by the court's findings, was that the Trial Judge failed in his duty under s.118 of the Evidence Act to conduct a proper preliminary examination and record his opinion on the child's capacity to understand questions, give rational answers, and understand the duty of speaking the truth.
respondent_arguments: The respondent supported the impugned judgments of the lower courts, implicitly arguing that the procedures followed, including the preliminary examination, were sufficient.

arguments.issue_text: Whether corroboration of the testimony of a child witness is a mandatory rule of law.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the conviction was unsafe because there was no support or corroboration for the testimony of the child witness (PW-1).
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that there is no rule that corroboration is necessary for maintaining a conviction on the sole testimony of a minor witness.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the preliminary examination of the child witness conducted by the Trial Court in the present case was adequate.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the preliminary examination was inadequate, describing it as 'very sketchy' and based on only three questions, which was insufficient to determine the child's competency.
respondent_arguments: The respondent supported the trial court's judgment, arguing that the child's testimony was reliable and that any alleged contradictions were insignificant, thereby implying the examination was adequate.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court must conduct a careful and cautious scrutiny of the evidence of a child witness, specifically applying its mind to the question of whether there is a possibility of the witness being tutored. The susceptibility of a child witness to tutoring is not, by itself, a ground to reject their evidence.
obiter: Corroboration of the testimony of a child witness is not a rule but a measure of caution and prudence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The conviction cannot be sustained because it is based solely on the testimony of a child witness (PW-1) which does not inspire confidence. This lack of confidence stems from the Trial Judge's failure to conduct a proper preliminary examination to establish the child's competency as required by Section 118 of the Evidence Act, the sketchy nature of the examination that was conducted, the un-ruled-out possibility that the child was tutored, and the absence of any corroborating evidence.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 118 of the Evidence Act, a Trial Judge has a duty to conduct a preliminary examination of a child witness and record his opinion that the child is able to understand the questions put to him, is able to give rational answers, and understands the duty of speaking the truth.
Corroboration of the testimony of a child witness is not a mandatory rule of law, but a measure of caution and prudence.
The court must conduct a careful scrutiny of the evidence of a child witness and apply its mind to the question of whether there is a possibility of the witness being tutored.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that a conviction is unsafe simply because there is no corroboration for a child witness's testimony was rejected as a matter of law. The court affirmed that corroboration is a rule of prudence, not a mandatory legal requirement.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued the legal principle that there is no absolute rule that corroboration is necessary to maintain a conviction based on the sole testimony of a minor witness. The court agreed, stating, 'It is a well-settled principle that corroboration of the testimony of a child witness is not a rule but a measure of caution and prudence.'
policy_considerations: The role of the Trial Judge in recording a child's evidence is crucial, and it is advisable to record the preliminary questions and answers so that an Appellate Court can properly review the correctness of the Trial Court's opinion on the child's competency.
While a child witness being susceptible to tutoring is not, by itself, a ground to reject their evidence, it necessitates that the court scrutinize their testimony with great care and caution.
